newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia rebels keep troops, demilitarization ends.
newsitem.headline: Colombia rebels keep troops, demilitarization ends.

text.p: President Ernesto Samper ordered the army to restart operations in a temporarily demilitarized zone of southern Colombia after leftist guerrillas failed to free 60 soldiers taken prisoner three months ago.

In a televised speech on Monday, Samper said the military would not be looking to rescue the captive troops by force nor to hunt down the rebels but added that normal manoeuvres would recommence at midnight Monday (0500 GMT Tuesday).

The president made the announcement four hours before the 10-day demilitarization of a 5,400-square-mile (14,000 sq km) area of Caqueta province officially ended. The government ordered troops out of the area on December 6 to allow the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) time to handover their captives and melt back into the jungles and mountains.

"Our offer was not a bargaining chip but a unilateral act of good faith to permit the release of the troops. But the FARC preferred to mount an international spectacle rather than listen to the lament of these young men's mothers," Samper said.

FARC rebels seized the soldiers, most of them raw recruits, when they overran a military base in neighbouring Putumayo province on August 30. The raid marked the start of one of the bloodiest guerrilla offensives in three decades of armed uprising.
In a communique sent from Mexico City earlier on Monday, FARC leaders reiterated their rejection of the government's terms for the handover.

"The lack of seriousness and sincerity (on the part of the government) and the abundance of insults and threats have become obstacles to the prompt and safe release of these troops," the statement said.
Although Samper did not give the green light to an all-out military offensive, defence experts military commanders may be planning just such an operation behind the scenes.

From the outset the government, and particularly the army, had been loath to hand what it saw as a propaganda opportunity to the FARC by getting bogged down in negotiations over terms for the troops' release.
